data.text:
F33 is at records 156 and 157, and unlike F32 it is **prevented and not merely detected**.
The contrast is the whole of this note, because note 154 had to say the opposite about the
statement one line above it in the same file.

## What is closed, measured rather than reasoned

Note 154 said sequences should differ from functions because PostgreSQL grants a sequence
nothing to PUBLIC, and said not to take that on trust. Measured on the reset database, on
PostgreSQL 17.6: after `alter default privileges for role postgres in schema public revoke
all on sequences from anon, authenticated`, a sequence created next is born
`{postgres=rwU/postgres,service_role=rwU/postgres}` with **no PUBLIC entry at all**;
`has_sequence_privilege('anon', ...)` is false for USAGE, SELECT and UPDATE alike; and
`nextval`, `select last_value` and `setval` are each refused 42501. The same holds for the
sequence a `bigint generated by default as identity` column creates, which is the route
SEEN-014 and SEEN-021 would take. So the prediction held, and prevention here is complete in
the way it is not for a function. That contrast is written into part 6 beside the statement.

The same limit as before does stand on the other grantor, measured this round rather than
assumed to carry over: `alter default privileges for role supabase_admin in schema public
revoke all on sequences ...` is refused 42501, so `supabase_admin`'s identical `S` entry is
still there and applies to a sequence `supabase_admin` itself creates, which nothing in this
repository does.

## One thing the RED found that the finding did not say

`nextval` and `setval` are outside transaction control. `anon` calling `setval(seq, 1)`
inside a statement that is then rolled back leaves the sequence at 1 afterwards; the probe
measures the value left behind and not only the answer the call got. So the write half of
F33 is a denial of service no rollback undoes, which is worse than "accepted" alone reads.

## `defaclobjtype = 'T'`, asked because the last four rounds each found the quarter before it

There is **no `T` row in `pg_default_acl` for schema public from either grantor**, so there
is nothing for part 6 to revoke, and `alter default privileges ... revoke all on types`
records no row when it is run. `anon` does hold USAGE on every type here, through the grant
PostgreSQL makes to PUBLIC on a type it creates, which no default privilege can reach,
exactly as for a function.

That one is harmless and the reason is asserted rather than left in prose: USAGE on a type is
not a route to a row. The probe creates a domain, shows `anon` holding USAGE on it and on the
row type of `public.tenants`, and shows `anon` still refused `select from public.tenants` with
42501, because reading rows goes through the table privilege part 4 governs. No type in this
schema holds data, and PostgREST serves no type as an endpoint, which is why `config.toml`
names four classes and not five. `T` is therefore in the detection, in
`DEFAULT_ACL_OBJECT_CLASSES` and in part 6's self-check, with no revoke beside it and the
reason stated there; what is asserted is only that no later migration files one.

With `S` and `T` in, the guard now reads the whole of `pg_default_acl` rather than the subset
a round happened to be looking at, which is the shape all four findings shared.

## Found and not fixed

- Note 154's three open items stand untouched: part 8's revoke list omits
  `seen.refuse_erasure_registry_mutation()`, `seen.touch_updated_at()` keeps its PUBLIC
  default, and **the suite still has no guard for schema `seen` at all**.
- Part 6's self-check for sequences spells `array['SELECT','UPDATE','USAGE']` inline where the
  suite reads `SEQUENCE_PRIVILEGES` from `tables.ts`. The migration cannot import TypeScript,
  so the duplication is structural, but nothing asserts the two lists agree. The same is true
  of the relkind and prokind lists already there; it is not a new asymmetry and it is not
  covered by any finding.
- F34 to F38 remain open and were not touched.
